items.text: Cohort studies link egg intake of up to one egg per day to higher cardiovascular disease risk in healthy adults
items.note: The reasoning is careful and genuinely independent, but the second subclaim is minted in the opposite direction from what the reasoning itself finds: it states meta-analyses DO find a significant positive association, while the prose says they report nulls — the graph now contains a child that, if ever funded, would "support" the claim by asserting something the steward concluded is false. This is a decomposition defect, not merely a stub. Secondary issues: the canonical form is ambiguous in exactly the way the assessment admits ("link" — whole literature vs. one pooled analysis), which a §3 rewrite should resolve rather than note; and with no web search, the verdict rests on recalled estimates (12%/16%, specific meta-analyses) that are hallucination-prone, though honestly flagged. Status contested at 0.7 with no credence is well calibrated for the live, split egg-CVD literature, and the importance of 0.5 is defensible.

items.text: Dietary cholesterol adversely affects the blood lipid profile.
items.note: The supported@0.85 verdict is honestly calibrated to an incomplete examination — the reasoning explicitly names why verified was not available, how skeptics were weighed without false parity, and what would flip the result — and the two requires-children are legitimate claims whose unassessed status costs nothing under §19. The real residual defect is that the load-bearing quantitative backbone (Hegsted/Keys equations, Clarke 1997, Mensink 2003, trial counts, mg/dL figures, the AHA/DGAC characterizations) is asserted from memory rather than examined sources, a contained but genuine hallucination risk the prose itself does not flag beyond the generic incompleteness disclaimer; stored importance 0.6 is also mildly high for a direction question that is close to settled among experts even if live in public discourse.

items.text: Eating up to one egg a day increases cardiovascular disease risk in healthy people.
items.note: The contested verdict and credence-vs-confidence split are well argued, but the stored claim text asserts harm causally at the affirmative pole while the assessment itself leans toward null (credence 0.3) — the text is stronger than the graph's own reading. Also, the reasoning rests on remembered meta-analyses with no evidence directly examined this run ("no web search was possible"), so 'contested' is grounded on background knowledge rather than examined sources; that is a defensible call but should be flagged as a verification gap.
